title: The wrong tool, correctly applied
spec: U04 · retrieve wide, ship narrow — and the question class where retrieval is the mistake
intro: Half of select is discipline: search the stacks, put three books on the desk. The other half is knowing when not to search at all. The grid has a clean case — a retrieval strategy that answers two questions perfectly for five times the price of just looking the rule up.
foot: Do it for real: Compare drawer on Q1 (naive vs jit), then on Q4 (graph vs okf)

steps.title: Wide belongs in the retriever, never in the window
narrative: Open the Compare drawer on Q1 — "Which criteria apply to procedure 72148 and what is the weight of each?" — with naive on the left and jit on the right.

Naive is the card catalog wheeled to your desk: 1,694 tokens, of which 1,612 are every record in the domain, serialized as JSON, so the model can go find the three rows about 72148. Jit is 143, and its receipt splits in two: a 54-token identifier index under tool results, and 7 tokens of retrieved records — because this question names a procedure, not a request, so almost nothing needed injecting.
Both answers are identical and both are ✓ verified. The difference is entirely in what got onto the desk.
steps.youDo: Compare drawer, pin Q1, left column naive, right column jit. Read the retrieved line on each.

after.title: JIT — an index, then the shortlist

steps.title: Two postures: cap what ships, or fetch on demand
narrative: Select shows up on the toggle bar in two different postures. budgeted assembles everything, then evicts whole records until the retrieved layer fits a cap — on Q1 that lands at 477 retrieved tokens, 559 total. Nothing is half-shipped: a record is either intact or gone, which is what keeps the surviving facts quotable.

jit ships an index of identifiers and injects only the records the question names. On Q9 you can read the two halves separately: the identifier index is the 54-token tool-results line, and the two request records it pulled in are the 78-token retrieved line. Total 220 against naive's 1,700.
Both are the same discipline — candidates are cheap, context slots are expensive. Budgeted decides at assembly time; jit defers the decision until the question has named something.

steps.title: The serialization tax
narrative: Before you tune which records ship, look at how they ship. Naive's retrieved layer is the seeded domain as pretty-printed JSON: braces, repeated field names, indentation, quoted keys on every row. Budgeted renders the same records as one flat line each and adds a policy line.

That is a formatting decision, not a retrieval decision, and it is worth a large multiple. Field names and punctuation can outweigh the facts they wrap — you can pay two tokens of scaffolding for every token of content and never notice, because the JSON looks tidy in a log.

The rule is dull and it works: ship records as the narrowest line that still carries the identifier and the fields the question needs. Keep the id verbatim; drop everything the answer key does not ask for.
steps.youDo: In the U04 lab, dump both retrieved layers to a file and diff them. Count how many of naive's tokens are punctuation and repeated keys.

steps.title: Where retrieval is the wrong tool
narrative: Now run a question whose answer is not hiding anywhere. Q4: "What is the eligibility rule, and which plan tier covers surgical procedures?" The answer is two sentences of stated policy — ACTIVE plan status, and only PREMIUM covers surgical.

Ask it in graph, the relationship-walking retriever, and it costs 1,054 input tokens. Ask it in okf, which loads a canonical concept file, and it costs 186. Same answer, word for word. Same ✓ verified stamp.

Q3 — the score thresholds — tells the same story a little more quietly: graph 840, okf 186. Nothing failed here. Graph is correct on both. It is correct at five and a half times the price, which is its own kind of bug.
steps.youDo: Compare drawer, pin Q4, left column graph, right column okf. Read both answers before you read either receipt.

steps.title: Why the graph inflated
narrative: This is not a mysterious retriever failure — it is a relevance test with an escape hatch. The graph assembler scans the question for entity mentions (a PA- id, an M- id, a procedure code) and for decision filters ("manual review", "denied", "eligib"), then renders the one-hop subgraph around whatever it found.

Q3 mentions both "manual review" and "denial", so every request with either decision gets rendered: 756 tokens of edges. Q4 mentions no entity at all — no request, no member, no procedure code — and the fallback branch treats everything as relevant. You get the whole graph, 970 tokens, because the question was too abstract to narrow on.

Read that as a general law about retrieval, not a quirk of this app: a retriever with no handle to grab widens. Canonical questions offer no handle by construction, which is exactly why they should never be routed to a retriever.

steps.title: Match the strategy to the question class
narrative: The takeaway is not "graph is bad" — on Q2 it is the tidiest retriever on the board. It is that retrieval strategy is a function of question class, and you can only know the mapping by grading it.

Fuzzy questions — which records look like this, what relates to what — deserve a retriever. Settled questions — what is the threshold, what is the rule, what does the policy say — deserve a lookup, because the fact was never lost and searching for it just buys you neighbours you did not ask for.

Before you reach for retrieval at all, ask one question: is this fact fuzzy enough to deserve a search, or settled enough to just state? Get that wrong and you pay 1,054 tokens for a two-line rule, and the receipt will congratulate you with a green stamp while you do it. U12 turns this table into a router.
steps.youDo: Run the full grid and build the class-to-strategy table yourself: python bench/run_campaign.py --modes graph,okf,jit,budgeted. Then argue with your own table.
